title: The DOM & Browser Events
description: Bridge the gap between JavaScript and HTML. Learn to query, create, modify, and delete DOM elements, then respond to user interaction through the browser's powerful event system.
learningObjectives: Query and traverse the DOM with querySelector and modern methods
Create, modify, and remove DOM elements
Understand event propagation: bubbling and capturing
Use event delegation for efficient event handling
Manipulate classes, attributes, and inline styles

exercises.question: Which method returns a live HTMLCollection (updates automatically if DOM changes)?
exercises.explanation: getElementsByClassName() (and getElementsByTagName()) return live HTMLCollections that automatically update when matching elements are added/removed. querySelectorAll() returns a static NodeList snapshot.

exercises.question: Why is el.textContent safer than el.innerHTML for displaying user-generated content?
options: textContent escapes HTML, preventing XSS attacks
innerHTML doesn't work in modern browsers
exercises.correctAnswer: textContent escapes HTML, preventing XSS attacks
hints: Think about what happens if a user enters <script>alert(1)</script>
exercises.explanation: textContent treats all content as literal text — tags are displayed as characters, not parsed. innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so malicious users could inject script tags (XSS).

exercises.question: What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
options: target is where the event started; currentTarget is where the listener is attached
currentTarget is the clickable element; target is the parent
target is for mouse events; currentTarget is for keyboard events
exercises.correctAnswer: target is where the event started; currentTarget is where the listener is attached
hints: A click on a span inside a button: target=span, currentTarget=button
exercises.explanation: event.target is the innermost element that triggered the event (where your click landed). event.currentTarget is always the element that has the addEventListener — it stays constant as events bubble.

sections.content: When an event fires on an element, it bubbles up through all ancestor elements in the DOM tree. This means a parent element can 'catch' events from its children.

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of event delegation over adding listeners to each element individually?
options: One listener handles current AND future elements, saving memory
exercises.correctAnswer: One listener handles current AND future elements, saving memory
exercises.explanation: Event delegation adds one listener to a parent. Because events bubble, all matching children (including dynamically added ones) are handled. This saves memory and eliminates the need to attach/detach listeners when items are added/removed.

exercises.question: Which Web Storage API retains data after the browser tab is closed?
exercises.explanation: localStorage persists indefinitely until explicitly cleared. sessionStorage is cleared when the browser tab is closed. For larger structured data, use IndexedDB.

capstoneProject.title: Interactive Kanban Board
capstoneProject.description: Build a drag-and-drop Kanban board using vanilla JavaScript and DOM APIs — no frameworks.
requirements: Three columns: Todo, In Progress, Done
Add task form using event listeners and DOM creation
Event delegation on each column for all task interactions
Drag and drop tasks between columns using dragstart/dragover/drop events
Delete task button on each card
Persist all tasks to localStorage (save/load on page load)
Animate cards entering viewport with IntersectionObserver
Task count badge on each column header (updates dynamically)
